How does being female change your access to education compared to the average?¶

In [43]:
import numpy as np


par_focus['Gender_Risk_Gap'] = par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls'] - par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for All']
par_focus['Gender_Risk_Ratio'] = np.where(
   par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for All'] == 0,
    np.nan,
   par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls'] / par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for All']
)

print("Descriptive Statistics of Risk Gap and Ratio (with NaNs handled):")
print(par_focus[['Gender_Risk_Gap', 'Gender_Risk_Ratio']].dropna().describe())

Descriptive Statistics of Risk Gap and Ratio (with NaNs handled):
       Gender_Risk_Gap  Gender_Risk_Ratio
count       107.000000         107.000000
mean          0.053084           1.695327
std           0.201158           1.647950
min          -0.500000           0.000000
25%          -0.071429           0.598214
50%           0.062500           1.285714
75%           0.155870           2.266667
max           0.700000           9.000000

The average Gender Risk Gap is approximately +5.3 percentage points, indicating that women and girls face a 5.3% higher risk of losing access to education compared to the general population. The mean Gender Risk Ratio is around 1.70, suggesting that girls and women have a 70% higher chance of being at risk than the average individual. The standard deviation is high (about 0.20 for gap, 1.65 for ratio) and reflects significant variation between different settings. There are instances where women have lower than average risk (min. gap of -0.5), although there are more instances of higher risk.

Percentage of cases where women face higher educational risk than the average: 55.68%

T-Test Result: t-statistic = 6.485, p-value = 0.000

  • The histogram shows that while many observations are clustered around zero gap, there is a noticeable right skew — meaning many cases have positive gender risk gaps (women facing higher risk). The mean line (red dashed) is shifted slightly right of zero, further supporting that women and girls are at greater risk overall.

  • Most of the data points lie above the equal risk line (the dashed red diagonal). This shows that, in the majority of cases, girls and women stand at higher risk than the overall population. Fewer than four observations lie below the line, indicating fewer instances where women pose lower risk.

  • From the boxplot, it can be observed that women and girls have a higher median risk than the population as a whole. The risk spread (interquartile range) is broader in women, signifying greater variation in the degree to which women's schooling is at risk. Outliers in everyone seem much lower than in females and girls, so extreme cases of high-risk recidivisms occur more frequently among females.

Risks to the Right to Education for Women and Girls by Country¶

## Calculating country based education risk gap for women over the time period
# Step 1: Filter the dataset for the two years of interest
par_focus_2018 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2018].copy()
par_focus_2019 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2019].copy()
par_focus_2020 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2020].copy()
par_focus_2021 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2021].copy()
par_focus_2022 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2022].copy()

# Step 2: Calculate education risk gap for women vs all
par_focus_2018['education_gender_gap'] = (
    par_focus_2018['Right to Education at Risk for All'] -
    par_focus_2018['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls'] 
    
)
par_focus_2019['education_gender_gap'] = (
    par_focus_2019['Right to Education at Risk for All'] -
    par_focus_2019['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls'] 
)
par_focus_2020['education_gender_gap'] = (
    par_focus_2020['Right to Education at Risk for All'] -
    par_focus_2020['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls']    
)
par_focus_2021['education_gender_gap'] = (
    par_focus_2021['Right to Education at Risk for All'] -
    par_focus_2021['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls']    
)
par_focus_2022['education_gender_gap'] = (
    par_focus_2022['Right to Education at Risk for All'] -
    par_focus_2022['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls'] 
)

Which countries had the largest shift in womens education rights risks over the 2018-2022 time period?¶

The education risk gap/education gender gap is the difference between the risks to education access for all in the population and the risks to education access for women and girls in the population. This tells us whether women and girls are better off, in-line with or worst off than the general population. Calculated as (Right to Education at Risk for All - Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls) When negative then women are at higher risk than the population at large When positive, then women are at lower risk than the overall population

In [47]:
## Finding the country with the largest shift over time
# Merge the two datasets and calculate absolute change
gap_comparison = pd.merge(
    par_focus_2018[['country', 'education_gender_gap']],
    par_focus_2022[['country', 'education_gender_gap']],
    on='country',
    suffixes=('_2018', '_2022')
)

gap_comparison['abs_change'] = (gap_comparison['education_gender_gap_2022'] - gap_comparison['education_gender_gap_2018']).abs()

# Identify the country with the largest absolute change
most_changed = gap_comparison.sort_values(by='abs_change', ascending=False)
most_changed.head()
Out[47]:
country education_gender_gap_2018 education_gender_gap_2022 abs_change
14 Jordan -0.500000 0.200000 0.700000
13 DRC -0.666667 -0.090909 0.575758
7 Mexico -0.571429 0.000000 0.571429
0 Angola -0.363636 0.100000 0.463636
9 Nepal 0.000000 -0.428571 0.428571

Jordan had the largest change in risk to women's education. In 2018 women were at higher risk with the gap (Education Risk to All - Risk to women) of -0.5. This meant the risks to women were higher than the risk to all. Now the gap has reversed with the risk to all being greater than the risk to women education and an absolute change of 0.7. This marks a drastic improvement in the status of women

Top 10 countries by absolute magnitude in change in education risks gap for women and girls¶

# Sort by absolute change, show top 10 changes
top_changes = gap_comparison.sort_values(by='abs_change', ascending=False).head(10)

# Set up bar color based on direction of change (improvement or worsening for women)
colors = ['green' if row['education_gender_gap_2022'] > row['education_gender_gap_2018'] else 'red'
          for _, row in top_changes.iterrows()]

# Create the bar plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.barh(top_changes['country'], top_changes['abs_change'], color=colors)
plt.xlabel('Absolute Change in Education Gender Gap (2018 to 2022) [2022 rate - 2018 rate]')
plt.ylabel('Countries')
plt.title('Top 10 Countries by Change in Education Risk Gap for Women')
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

green = improvement in the status of women, red = decline in the status of women

When we plot the largest absolute changes we see that Nepal is the country with the largest deterioration in the education rights of women and girls since 2018

# Calculate gender gap
par_focus['education_gender_gap'] = (
    par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for All'] -
    par_focus['Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls']
)

# Filter years 2018–2022
filtered = par_focus[par_focus['year'].between(2018, 2022)]

# Compute average gap by country
avg_gap_by_country = filtered.groupby('country')['education_gender_gap'].mean()

# Separate countries into negative vs positive gap lists
negative_gap_countries = avg_gap_by_country[avg_gap_by_country < 0].index.tolist()
positive_gap_countries = avg_gap_by_country[avg_gap_by_country > 0].index.tolist()

Which country/countries is showing the biggest improvement for females’ rights to education across the last 5 years?¶

In [52]:
# Filter necessary columns
edu_female = par_focus[['country', 'year', 'Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls']].dropna()

# For each country, get earliest and latest value within the last 5 years
latest_year = edu_female['year'].max()
five_years_ago = latest_year - 5

recent_data = edu_female[edu_female['year'] >= five_years_ago]
In [53]:
# Get change over time per country
change = (
    recent_data
    .sort_values(['country', 'year'])
    .groupby('country')
    .agg(first_year=('year', 'first'),
         last_year=('year', 'last'),
         start_val=('Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls', 'first'),
         end_val=('Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls', 'last'))
    .assign(change=lambda x: x['start_val'] - x['end_val'])  # drop in par_focus = improvement
    .sort_values('change', ascending=False)
)

# Display top improving country
top_improver = change.iloc[0]
print(f"Country with biggest improvement: {top_improver.name}")
print(f"Drop in par_focus over 5 years: {top_improver['change']:.2f}")

Country with biggest improvement: DRC
Drop in par_focus over 5 years: 0.68
In [54]:
# Visualization - Barplot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

change.head(10).plot(kind='barh', y='change', title='Top 10 Countries: Improvement in Education Risk for Women')
plt.xlabel('Decrease in Risk (Proportion Points)')
plt.ylabel('Country')
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Between 2018 and 2023, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) showed the greatest improvement in women and girls’ access to education. Specifically, the proportion of survey respondents identifying women and girls as being at par_focus of being denied the right to education decreased by 68 percentage points over this five-year period.

2018 vs 2022 Change in Risks to Women's Access to Education by Continent¶

# STEP 2: Apply mapping to entire dataset

par_focus_2018['continent'] = par_focus_2018['country'].map(relevant_country_continent_map)
par_focus_2022['continent'] = par_focus_2022['country'].map(relevant_country_continent_map)

# STEP 4: Group by continent and compute mean gaps
continent_gap_2018 = par_focus_2018.groupby('continent', as_index=False)['education_gender_gap'].mean()
continent_gap_2022 = par_focus_2022.groupby('continent', as_index=False)['education_gender_gap'].mean()

# STEP 5: Merge and calculate changes
continent_gap_change = pd.merge(continent_gap_2018, continent_gap_2022, on='continent', suffixes=('_2018', '_2022'))
continent_gap_change['change'] = continent_gap_change['education_gender_gap_2022'] - continent_gap_change['education_gender_gap_2018']

# STEP 6: Plot

continent_gap_change_sorted = continent_gap_change.sort_values(by='change', ascending=False)
colors = ['green' if val > 0 else 'red' for val in continent_gap_change_sorted['change']]

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.barh(continent_gap_change_sorted['continent'], continent_gap_change_sorted['change'], color=colors)
plt.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=0.8, linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel("Change in Education Gender Gap (2022 - 2018)")
plt.title("Change in Education Gender Gap by Continent (All − Women)")
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# STEP 1: Rebuild year-specific slices
par_focus_2018 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2018].copy()
par_focus_2019 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2019].copy()
par_focus_2020 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2020].copy()
par_focus_2021 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2021].copy()
par_focus_2022 = par_focus[par_focus['year'] == 2022].copy()

# STEP 2: Combine into a unified DataFrame
par_focus_combined = pd.concat([
    par_focus_2018.assign(year=2018),
    par_focus_2019.assign(year=2019),
    par_focus_2020.assign(year=2020),
    par_focus_2021.assign(year=2021),
    par_focus_2022.assign(year=2022)
])

# STEP 3: Apply continent mapping
par_focus_combined['continent'] = par_focus_combined['country'].map(relevant_country_continent_map)

# STEP 4: Group and pivot for line chart
trend_grouped = par_focus_combined.groupby(['year', 'continent'], as_index=False)[
    'Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls'
].mean()

trend_pivot = trend_grouped.pivot(index='year', columns='continent', values='Right to Education at Risk for Women and Girls')

# STEP 5: Plot line chart cleanly using Axes object
ax = trend_pivot.plot(
    figsize=(12, 6),
    marker='o',
    linewidth=2,
    markersize=6
)

# Format plot labels, title, and legend
ax.set_title('Education Risk to Women by Continent (2018–2022)', fontsize=14)
ax.set_ylabel('Avg. Education Risk for Women and Girls')
ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.grid(True)

# Move legend outside the plot area
ax.legend(title='Continent', loc='center left', bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5))

# Adjust layout to prevent clipping
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

While Africa was the most improved it must also be noted that Africa has consistently lead the world in risks to women and girls. Europe and Oceania have the lowest risk to women and girls followed by North America

From the provided statistical summary, we can conclude the following:¶

For all:¶

  • The mean risk is relatively low at 0.1076, indicating that, on average, the risk to education for all is minimal.
  • The standard deviation is 0.1339, showing moderate variability in the data.

For Women and Girls:¶

  • The mean risk is higher at 0.1994, indicating that women and girls face more educational risks compared to the general population.
  • The standard deviation is 0.1786, indicating higher variability compared to the general population.

For Lower Social Classes:¶

  • The mean risk is the highest at 0.4306, suggesting that lower social classes face the most significant educational risks.
  • The standard deviation is 0.2024, showing considerable variability in the data.

Conclusion:¶

  • Lower social classes face the highest educational risks, followed by women and girls, and then the general population.
  • There is significant variability in the risks across all groups, with some cases showing very high risks.

  • There is a strong positive correlation between health & education for lower classes, indicates that where lower-status groups face higher risks to health rights, they likewise tend to face notably higher risks to education rights.

  • Similarly, correlation between food & education for lower classes shows that areas with greater food rights risk for lower-status groups also generally experience elevated risks to educationfor those same groups.

Looking at the correlations by the top 3 countries most risky for education rights¶

In [66]:
# Define the selected countries (example list, replace with actual countries)
selected_countries = ['Mexico', 'United States', 'Brazil']

# Filter data for the selected countries
filtered_data = par_focus[par_focus['country'].isin(selected_countries)]

# Initialize a dictionary to store the results
correlations = {}

# Loop through each country and calculate correlations
for country in selected_countries:
    country_data = filtered_data[filtered_data['country'] == country]
    
    # Calculate correlation between health and education
    health_edu_corr = country_data[
        ['Right to Education at Risk for Lower Social Classes', 'Right to Health at Risk for Lower Social Classes']
    ].corr().iloc[0, 1]
    
    # Calculate correlation between food and education
    food_edu_corr = country_data[
        ['Right to Education at Risk for Lower Social Classes', 'Right to Food at risk for Lower Social Classes']
    ].corr().iloc[0, 1]
    
    # Store the results
    correlations[country] = {
        'Health vs Education': health_edu_corr,
        'Food vs Education': food_edu_corr
    }

# Convert correlations dictionary to DataFrame for plotting
cor_df = pd.DataFrame(correlations).T

# Plotting
ax = cor_df.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10, 6), rot=0)
plt.title("Correlation of Health and Food Risk with Education Risk (Lower Social Classes)")
plt.ylabel("Correlation Coefficient")
plt.ylim(0, 1.05)
plt.legend(title="Correlation Type")
plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)

# Add data labels
for container in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(container, fmt='%.2f', label_type='edge', fontsize=10)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

  • In the United States, there’s a very strong link between food, health, and education risks. When food or healthcare access is limited, education for lower-income people is also heavily affected.

  • In Mexico, health and education risks are somewhat connected, but food access doesn’t seem to relate much to education risk.

  • In Brazil, the connections between food, health, and education risks are weaker, suggesting that other issues like politics or regional differences may matter more.
